Lees
LEEZ
noun (plural)
From the Old French lie, the sediment of wine, of Celtic origin. The lees are the dregs that settle at the bottom of a wine vessel; wine left long upon its lees grows strong and clear, but the same stillness that refines good wine sours bad.

Biblical Definition

Lees are wine-sediment, and Scripture makes brilliant double use of the image. On the one hand, wine aged upon the lees is the finest wine, and so it appears in the great banquet promise: “in this mountain shall the LORD of hosts make unto all people a feast of fat things, a feast of wines on the lees, of fat things full of marrow, of wines on the lees well refined” (Isa 25:6). Note well refined — the wine has rested long and been drawn off clear. On the other hand, the same settling describes a soul that has never been disturbed. Moab “hath been at ease from his youth, and he hath settled on his lees, and hath not been emptied from vessel to vessel” (Jer 48:11), and the verse ends devastatingly: therefore his taste remained in him, and his scent is not changed. Moab was never poured out, never uprooted, never carried captive — and so never changed. Undisturbed prosperity preserved him exactly as he was. Zephaniah applies the same figure to Jerusalem: God will “search Jerusalem with candles, and punish the men that are settled on their lees: that say in their heart, The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil” (Zep 1:12). That is practical atheism in a sentence — not the denial of God’s existence but of His activity, the settled conviction of a comfortable man that heaven is indifferent.

Webster 1828 Definition

The sediment or dregs of wine, settling at the bottom of the vessel; used both of wine long refined and of a soul left undisturbed and therefore unchanged.

LEES, n. plural. The grosser parts of liquor which settle at the bottom; dregs; sediment.

From the Old French lie, dregs; of Celtic origin.

Wine left upon the lees and then drawn off is strengthened and clarified (Isa 25:6).

To be settled on the lees is to remain long undisturbed in one vessel (Jer 48:11).

Figuratively, of a man grown thick and unchanged through ease.

Key Scripture

Isa 25:6 — "And in this mountain shall the LORD of hosts make unto all people a feast of fat things, a feast of wines on the lees, of fat things full of marrow, of wines on the lees well refined."

Jer 48:11 — "Moab hath been at ease from his youth, and he hath settled on his lees, and hath not been emptied from vessel to vessel, neither hath he gone into captivity: therefore his taste remained in him, and his scent is not changed."

Zep 1:12 — "And it shall come to pass at that time, that I will search Jerusalem with candles, and punish the men that are settled on their lees: that say in their heart, The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil."

Psa 55:19 — "God shall hear, and afflict them, even he that abideth of old. Selah. Because they have no changes, therefore they fear not God."

Modern Corruption

An untroubled life is read as a sign of divine favour, when Jeremiah names undisturbed ease as the very reason Moab’s taste remained in him and his scent was not changed.

expand to see more

The corruption is the equation of ease with blessing. It is nearly universal, and it is refuted in one of the sharpest verses in the prophets. Moab had everything a man could pray for — at ease from his youth, never emptied from vessel to vessel, never gone into captivity — and Jeremiah presents the whole record as an indictment. The unbroken calm did not sanctify him; it fixed him. Therefore his taste remained in him, and his scent is not changed. The very absence of upheaval preserved every fault he had at twenty into his old age. The Psalmist says the same of men who have no changes: therefore they fear not God (Psa 55:19).

Recover the plain sense: God empties His people from vessel to vessel on purpose. The disturbances a Christian resents — the move, the loss, the illness, the reversal — are frequently the pouring that keeps him from thickening on his lees. This is not a doctrine that romanticises suffering, nor does it promise that every trouble improves a man; the fool in the mortar is answer enough to that. But it does forbid reading a smooth life as a certificate. Zephaniah names the end state precisely: men settled on their lees say in their heart The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil — a God who is real, and irrelevant. Against that, set Isa 25:6, where the wine on the lees is well refined, kept long and then drawn off clear. There is a settling that ruins and a settling that matures, and the difference is whether the vessel was ever tipped.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old French lie, sediment — the dregs beneath the wine; the figure of ease that thickens a soul, and of wine long refined.

Lees — Old French lie, the sediment of wine.

Wine long upon the lees and drawn off clear is the strongest (Isa 25:6).

Jer 48:11: Moab settled on his lees, never emptied from vessel to vessel.

The result: his taste remained in him, and his scent is not changed.

Zep 1:12: settled men say the LORD will do neither good nor evil.
